name: Praying Mantis
description: The only known invertebrate with stereoscopic 3D vision, using binocular disparity for precise depth perception during prey strikes. Raptorial forelegs execute strikes in 50-70 milliseconds — among the fastest predatory movements in the insect world. Head rotation of 180 degrees provides a wide surveillance field from a stationary ambush position. Masters patience as strategy: stillness as computation, waiting as optimization.

core_attributes.neurology: stereoscopic vision, rapid strike motor circuits
core_attributes.pattern: 3D binocular vision, ambush patience, ultra-fast raptorial strike

scope.definition: Depth discrimination accuracy of praying mantis stereo vision — minimum detectable depth difference between two targets at 10 cm range, expressed as fraction of inter-target distance.

evidence.source: Rossel (1983) 'Binocular stereopsis in an insect', Nature 302:821-822; Nityananda et al. (2016) 'Insect stereopsis demonstrated using a 3D insect cinema', Scientific Reports 6:18718.
cross_domain_examples: mantis detects 0.3 mm depth difference at 10 cm — resolution matched to strike precision requirement
unique insect stereo vision: the only non-vertebrate with confirmed binocular depth computation
human stereo vision: 0.1 mm depth resolution at 30 cm — mantis scales linearly with prey-strike range

scope.falsifiability: If mantis strike success on moving targets is statistically identical when one eye is occluded vs binocular conditions, stereoscopic depth processing is not contributing to strike accuracy.
scope.measurement_limits: Stereoscopic depth computation only functional for objects within 30 cm — beyond this range mantis uses motion parallax. Operates in temporal domain (motion-based stereo) rather than disparity-based stereo.

scope.definition: Strike accuracy of mantis raptorial foreleg — fraction of strikes where foreleg contacts prey within 2 mm of midthorax (optimal grip point), measured by high-speed camera at 3000 fps.

evidence.source: Corrette (1990) 'Prey capture in the praying mantis', Journal of Experimental Biology 148:287-306; Loxton & Nicholls (1979) mechanics of mantis prey capture.
cross_domain_examples: mantis foreleg strike velocity 0.1 m/s to 1.5 m/s in 20-30 ms — equivalent to 9-17 G acceleration
strike accuracy 0.88-0.94 for prey within 3 cm, drops to 0.62 for prey beyond 5 cm
pistol shrimp dactyl closure: fastest limb strike in nature (0.9 ms) — convergent raptorial appendage evolution

scope.falsifiability: If high-speed video analysis shows foreleg contact points distributed randomly over prey body rather than concentrated at thorax, optimal grip-point targeting is not occurring.
scope.measurement_limits: Accuracy is prey-size dependent — small flies vs large beetles require different foreleg timing. Strike accuracy decreases 25% in sub-optimal illumination. Mantis uses visual peaking behavior to increase accuracy.

scope.definition: Energetic advantage of mantis sit-and-wait predation — ratio of calories acquired per hour to active-hunting equivalent, measured as prey encounter rate per unit energy expenditure during 24h monitoring.

evidence.source: Ehrmann (2002) 'Mantodea: Gottesanbeterinnen der Welt', Natur und Tier Verlag; Caraco & Chasin (1984) foraging preferences in ambush vs pursuit strategies.
cross_domain_examples: crypsis + sit-and-wait reduces energy expenditure 60-80% vs active search, while prey encounter rate 0.72 of active hunting
overall energy return: sit-and-wait 2.2× higher caloric return per unit metabolic cost than active pursuit
ambush spider (Misumena): 2.8× higher energy return than web-building alternative in same habitat

scope.falsifiability: If mantids kept in active-movement forcing experiments (no stationary perches) show equivalent or higher prey capture rates than sit-and-wait individuals, patience does not provide foraging advantage.
scope.measurement_limits: Sit-and-wait advantage depends on prey density and distribution. In sparse prey environments, active search is necessary. Measurement requires comparing matched mantids with vs without perch access over 72h.
